summary: The Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge asks for an intuitive way to compare landing sites and dates near the Moon's south pole, where sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth for communication are scarce and constantly shifting. Moonview is that comparison tool. It puts the challenge's core questions in one place: how high does the Sun get above the horizon, how long does it stay up, when is Earth visible, and how do those answers change from site to site and date to date. Because mission plans slip, it treats replanning as the normal case, letting planners swap sites or dates and immediately see the effect on feasibility. And because the challenge names educators and the public alongside planners, it explains through clear visuals instead of specialist interfaces. Better site decisions, made faster, mean missions that stay powered and stay in contact.
details:
Moonview - Lunar Site Platform

Moonview is a website we built to help people understand and compare potential landing sites on the Moon. The idea was to bring several different planning tools into one place so users can easily see how sunlight, Earth visibility, and lunar nights affect different locations.

The website includes multiple tools, each serving a different purpose. Year at a Glance shows how sunlight and Earth visibility change throughout the year, while Day Path breaks down these conditions hour by hour for a single day. Storage Sizing estimates how much battery storage a location would need to get through its longest nights. Site Scoreboard ranks different locations based on sunlight, Earth visibility, and night length, and Site Comparison lets users compare any two locations side by side. We also built an interactive 3D Moon view and included historical Apollo mission information for reference.

For the actual calculations, we used elevation data from NASA's LOLA instrument to model the lunar surface. We then calculate whether the Sun and Earth are above or below the local horizon at different locations and times. Everything runs directly in the browser, so users can get results without waiting for a server to process anything.

The main goal was to make lunar site selection easier to understand. Instead of having to look through different datasets and calculate everything separately, users can use Moonview to narrow down potential sites and see the tradeoffs between them. For example, one location might have longer periods of sunlight, while another might have better visibility of Earth for communication.

One important thing we made sure to include is that our results are based on modeled geometry, not guaranteed real-world conditions. We make this clear throughout the website so users understand what the calculations actually represent.

Technologies Used: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Python, NASA LOLA elevation data, GitHub, and Vercel.

Team Stratosphere: Yousha Ahmed and Noah Krauss
